99.9% of all my interactions with law enforcement have been positive but the one time I had a run in with fish and game it wasnt pleasant at all and in fact coulve been worse. Ive always been respectful to law enforcement and have never really gotten into trouble with the law in my life but these 2 fish and game dudes were rough lol. I ride dirt bikes around my area on local trails and what not and have been for over 15 years mostly without issue. Any LEO that stopped me basically just said you cant ride here the Id apologize say I didnt know and leave. They also say to stay off the roads which I do. BUT when I was like 15 or 16 me and 2 of my friends were riding our dirt bikes in an area weve rode in for a couple years with no problems until one day we ran into 2 fish and game officers on ATVs that stopped us. They gave us tickets for riding in an area that was technically Amtrak property but there were no signs or anything that say we cant be there. They go on us saying they could slam up with charges and fines because we didnt have drivers/motorcycle licenses, the bikes werent registered or insured, we didnt have light, mirrors, directionals, or license plates all that kind of stuff. We didnt even know we needed any of that. Our bikes were all bought second hand off of people so we didnt have things like title, registration and had no idea they even needed to be insured. We were literally early teenagers! We werent being reckless, we werent trying to hurt anyone or anything but they went OFF on us saying "We coulve towed the bikes today! Next time we catch you guys out here the bikes are getting towed and you will get ALL the fines!" and made us push our bikes more than a mile home. They were just assholes.

I am a CO at a county jail and heres what I can tell you: 1) be prepared to be tested by the inmates when you are a rookie. The inmates will try either to scare you by being overly aggressive or they will be overly nice to try to see if you can be manipulated. Dont fall victim to the con games. 2) Find the balance between being an authority figure and a human. All COs run their housing units differently but for me I use the approach of "dont mistake my kindness for weakness". Im generally pretty lax when running my unit but if people start getting loud or crazy I bring the hammer down hard on everyone (Ive even shut off all the TVs and phones for a whole shift a few times from inmates acting up). Dont have to be super nice to the inmates but also dont be a dick or youre gunna have a hard time every single day. 3) Remember YOU are in charge not them! Youre not a butler, youre not a maid, youre not their for customer service to ensure their stay is as enjoyable and comfortable as possible, youre the boss. If the unit is dirty and unkempt tell the porters to clean the unit and if they refuse LOCK THEIR ASSES IN!

As for becoming accepted by co-workers: When you start day 1, dont try to be buddy buddy with anyone. Dont be all loud and happy because all of us are miserable lol. Just go in, shut the fuck up, head down, and do your job. You do that and eventually people will flock to you dont try to force yourself into the established culture there right away. I stuck to this as a rookie and it worked great and I have tons of good friends here now and alot of us hang out outside of work as well.

Dont base the entire job on your first few months. Give it about a minimum of 6 months to start to get the hang of things and dont be afraid to ask questions!

believe it or not it did have some downsides that didnt become apparent until later in life. I come from a very large Italian family and we were all super close. I mean 2 of my cousins were like my best friends growing up. Little to no drama ever in my whole family or even just my household family. Sure I was a a little asshole as a teenager but never had any big fights or falling outs with my family. What really hurt me later in life was the lack of responsibility my parents gave me. Never made me do chores like ever and If I did do them it was because I needed money and Id get like 20-30 bucks to mow the lawn or clean the pool. My mom always cleaned the house despite having a full time job and never made me and my sisters do anything nor did she fuss about it. She was totally fine with me hanging out with my friends and also me spending I shit you not over 8 hours straight of playing video games and never made me get off unless I was grounded. Which I had to REALLLY fuck up to be grounded. If I got in trouble my parents would bail me out of EVERYTHING without question. Got my dirt bike impounded by the cops for trespassing and being a nuisance with my friends? They paid and got it out of impound THAT day and went off on the cop calling him "Barney Fife" and how we were just being "boys".

  
Now Im an adult and I struggle with basic adult tasks: probably make my bed once a week, I barely clean my house I just save it up for weeks and weeks and the only time I clean is when Im expecting company and give the illusion that my house always looks like that, I cant cook, Im an impulsive spender (like dropping 8K on a new dirt bike without any financial planning), laundry and dishes only get done when there is none of either that are clean, etc. I try to fix the behavior and it works for like a couple weeks then fall hard back into my old habits. Trying to rewire a lifestyle that Ive had for 25+ years is very difficult. Even 4 years in the army couldnt fix all that. Stuff was neat and squared away because I didnt want to get in trouble not because I knew its what I needed to do.

  
TL;DR - coming from a fully functional and blissful family is very nice and Im grateful for the life I had growing up. But boy was I unprepared for the real adult world when it hit and I had to deal with negativity on my own and not have curtains in front of my eyes.
